descr.name: qHTS for Suppressors of FUS Proteinopathy: Primary screen using FUS-linked yeast assay
description: Several widespread neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer disease, Huntington disease, Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration (FTLD) and Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), share a common pathological feature, namely accumulation of specific protein aggregates in diseased tissue. These diseases which is associated with protein misfolding (proteinopathies) have become increasingly problematic as the population ages and life expectancies are extended.  Most proteinopathies are currently incurable, a situation confounded by the fact that the basis of neurodegeneration is generally poorly understood.  There exists urgent and significant need to find therapeutics that can inhibit the toxicity associated with protein aggregation. A novel approach to understand the underlying mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases has recently emerged in which the disease conditions are modeled in the yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), a tractable eukaryotic organism with conserved protein quality control mechanisms. Yeast offers quick and reliable genetic manipulations and can be easily tailored to high-throughput screening (HTS).

For this project, a yeast model of the FUS proteinopathies (a spectrum of neurodegenerative diseases that include ALS and a subtype of FTLD) was generated and employed. The cytoplasmic accumulation of the DNA/RNA-binding protein FUS (also known as TLS) is causative to both familial and sporadic forms of ALS and FTLD.  This yeast model recapitulates neuronal pathology by showing severe cytotoxicity associated with cytoplasmic accumulation of FUS aggregates and a specific interaction between FUS and TDP-43, another ALS-associated protein.  The mechanism of this model was observed to be like the FUS toxicity mechanism in a variety of organisms.  Specifically, the cellular accumulation of misfolded FUS that disrupts RNA homeostasis in both yeast and higher eukaryotes. This model was validated to be suitable for quantitative HTS (qHTS) use for finding genetic or chemical factors that restore growth. The assay was run against the MLPCN compound library collection and had a read-out as activators which indicated increase in absorbance (OD) signal. Identified compounds that inhibits FUS-yeast toxicity is flagged, re-acquired, and validated for further investigation and optimization.
NIH Molecular Libraries Probe Production Centers Network [MLPCN]
Assay Submitter (PI): Frank Shewmaker PhD, Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences
protocol: Reagents / Controls:

Compound CP55940 was used as the positive control. Column 1 was treated with CP55940 titration from 92uM (final concentration, 1:2 dilution), while Column 2 was treated with top dose 92uM. Columns 3 and 4 were treated with DMSO only as negative control to assess background and noise signal.
Assay Steps:

Four hundred fifty microliter of cultured yeast (in 20mL rich medium) provided by Dr. Shewmaker lab was incubated at 30C at 99% humidity for 3hr. The culture was then spun down at 4000rpm for 5min and the cell pellet was resuspended in 2mL of Sdmin Media + ALU(330) + 2.5% Raffinose. One hundred microliter of the suspension was added to 900uL of water and OD of the solution was obtained. Twenty mL of responding medium (provided by Shewmaker lab) + 2.5% raffinose was added to ensure cell density of 0.1; the solution was incubated overnight. Working cell solution (FUS-yeast in Sdmi + Sdmi + 1X ALU + 2% galactose media) was prepared (final OD at 0.005) and 3uL was dispensed in a 1536-well Aurora high based clear bottom assay plates. Controls and library compounds (at various final concentrations from 40uM to 0.32uM) were added using a 1536-well pin array using the Kalypsys pin-tool. The plates were then incubated for 24hrs in a cell-culture incubator (30C; 99% humidity). Absorbance at 600nM was then read using the PerkinElmer ViewLux plate reader. Data was normalized to the cells + DMSO only wells and compounds exhibiting similar rescue response curve exhibited by the control CP55940 were flagged and cherrypicked for validation and further investigation.

descr.name: qHTS Assay for Foot and Mouth Disease Virus Antivirals: Primary Screen against the MLPCN compound library
description: Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus (FMDV) is a picornavirus that infects cloven-hoofed animals and leads to severe losses in livestock production.  Like many picornaviruses, FMDV uses an unusual form of decoding called StopGo or Stop-Carry on (or formerly "2A").  In StopGo there is non-standard release of an upstream encoded protein when there is a glycine codon in the ribosomal P-site (Stop) and continued translation (Go) with the proline encoded by the A-site codon being the N-terminal amino acid of a downstream encoded protein i.e. two tandemly encoded proteins without an intervening stop codon or conventional re-initiation.  StopGo is completely dependent on a highly conserved amino acid motif DxExNP immediately N-terminal to the G / P.  In a recent publication by Gary Loughran et al, it was described that the StopGo appears to be essential for the foot and mouth virus viability [1]. In addition, this sequence is 100% conserved among all known subtypes (~60) of FMDV and thus provides an attractive target for potential FMDV antiviral treatment.  There are currently no approved anti-FMDV drugs for the treatment or prevention of FMDV.

An FMDV StopGo NPG Luciferase reporter assay was developed by Dr. Atkins lab and optimized for quantitative high throughput screen (qHTS) to identify inhibitors of FMDV StopGo. This assay targeted the resumption of translation on P ("Go") rather than the termination at G ("Stop"). The assay was run against the MLPCN compound library collection and decrease in luciferase signal is the desired outcome for this assay. Identified compounds that exhibit greater than 50% inhibition was flagged, re-acquired, and validated for further investigation and medicinal chemistry optimization.
NIH Molecular Libraries Probe Production Centers Network [MLPCN]
Assay Submitter (PI): John Atkins PhD, University of Utah

[1] Loughran, G., et al. Theiler's murine encephalomyelitis virus contrats with encephalomycarditis and foot-and-mouth disease viruses in its functional utilization of the StopGo non-standrad translation mechanism. Journal of General Virology (2013), 94, 348-353.

Dose response was assessed using a 1:2 dilution of control compound, with the top dose of 50uM final concentration. Background signal was normalized to wells treated with DMSO only.
Assay Protocol:

In brief, 3000 HEK-NPGP-Luc cells were plated overnight before adding 23nL of FireFly inhibitors per well using a pintool workstation (Kalypsys) followed by incubation for 4 hr.  Luciferase activity was then measured using Amplite Luciferase Reagent.

descr.name: Primary screen GU AMC qHTS for Zika virus inhibitors
description: Avindra Nath, Ph.D., National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), Bethesda, MD
Radhakrishnan Padmanabhan, Ph.D., Georgetown University (GU), Washington D.C.

Zika Virus causes congenital defects, including microcephaly and is associated with Guillain-Barre syndrome, eningoencephalitis and myelitis in infected adult. Presently, there are efforts underway to develop a vaccine, but there are no treatments for those who have been infected or are demonstrating symptoms. Using a target-based approach, we hope to establish a screening paradigm to uncover novel, cell-active NS2B-NS3 protease (Zika Virus) specific inhibitors from NCATS' collection of small molecules using qHTS. These results can then be used to determine potential probe(s) for further characterization as potential treatment for patients.
National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS), Rockville, MD
National Institute of Health (NIH), Bethesda, Maryland
protocol: Padmanabhan lab provided the NS2B hydrophilic domain and NS3 protease domain in a noncovalent complex used for the unlinked assay. Control compound aprotinin is obtained from Thermo Scientific (#78432; Waltham, Massachusetts). NS2B-NS3 AMC substrate (Bz-Nle-Lys-Arg-Arg-AMC; Nle-KRR-AMC) purchased from Bachem (#I-1995; Torrance, CA). Ac-VKTGKR-AMC purchased from Genscript or Bachem, Ac-FAAGKR-AMC purchased from Genscript, Ac-GLVKRR-AMC purchased from Genscript, Ac-LKKR-AMC purchased from Genscript.
GU AMC unlinked NS2B-NS3 protease qHTS protocol

Briefly, 3 microL of Zika virus unlinked NS2B-NS3 protease (25 nM for linked final concentration), in assay buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 with 0.01% Tween 20) was dispensed into a 1,536-well solid-bottom black plate (Greiner Bio One, Monroe, NC). Twenty-three nL of compounds (final concentration range 7.28 nM to 114 microM) or control Aprotinin (final concentration range 3.47 nM to 114 microM) were transferred via Wako Pin-tool (Wako Automation, Richmond, VA). Samples were incubated (room temperature, protected from light) for 15 minutes followed by a 1 microL AMC substrate addition of (final concentration of 10 microM; Km = 18.3 muM). Plates were then read immediately on a ViewLux High-throughput CCD imager (PerkinElmer, Waltham, MA) equipped with standard UV fluorescence optics (340(30) nm excitation, 450(20) nm emission) then incubated (room temperature, protected from light) for 15 minutes (~20% conversion). The change in fluorescence intensity over the 15-minute reaction period was normalized against no-inhibitor and no-enzyme controls and the resulting percent inhibition data were fitted to a 4-parameter Hill equation. Aprotinin was used as the intraplate control.

descr.name: Primary screen for KDM5B Histone Demethylases FDH-coupled qHTS
description: Assay Submitter (PI): Qin Yan, Ph.D. (Yale University) and Xiaodong Cheng, Ph.D. (MD Anderson)
This project was funded as part of the NCI NEXT Program and Chemical Biology Consortium (CBC)
The histone demethylases, KDM5A and KDM5B catalyze the demethylation of lysine 4 on histone H3 (H3K4me3/2). They

are overexpressed in a variety of cancers and have been implicated in cancer cell growth, metastasis, drug resistance, and tumor growth. KDM5A is amplified and overexpressed in breast and gastric cancer; and is translocated in leukemia. While KDM5B is highly expressed in human mammary tumors and breast cancer cell lines, but not in normal adult breast tissue. Moreover, knockdown of KDM5B leads to upregulation of tumor suppressor genes, including BRCA1. The goal of this project is to employ qHTS to identify selective small molecule inhibitors of KDM5A/B demethylase activity to better understand the role of KDM5 in cancer and to develop novel therapies.

We employed an FDH-coupled assay previously reported by Sakurai et al. [1] to monitor in vitro KDM5 demethylase activity. Compounds showing dose response inhibition are re-acquired, validated, and tested for non-specific interference with the formaldehyde dehydrogenase (FDH) counterscreen. True inhibitors are validated using an AlphaLisa secondary screen, which employs an H3K4(me2-1)-specific antibody to monitor demethylation of a biotin-tagged H3K4(me3) peptide substrate. Inhibitors are profiled against KDM4A and KDM6A AlphaLisa counterscreens to determine level of demethylase specificity; and against the TruHits counterscreen to eliminate non-specific inhibitory activity on the AlphaLISA detection method. Selective inhibitors identified from the primary and secondary screening are tested in cells using immunofluorescence to monitor global H3K4 tri-methylation as a measure of KDM5A/B inhibition.
National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences (NCATS), Rockville, MD
National Institute of Health (NIH), Bethesda, Maryland
[1] Sakurai, M et al. A miniaturized screen for inhibitors of Jumonji histone demethylases. Mol Biosyst. 2010 Feb;6(2):357-64. doi: 10.1039/b912993f. Epub 2009 Oct 8.
protocol: Materials:

1536-well Black, solid bottom, medium binding assay plate is purchased from Greiner Bio-one. The enzymes (KDM5B) and substrate (H3K4me3/2) are provided by the principal investigators. The buffer for this assay is composed of 50mM HEPES at pH 7.5 with 0.01% Tween-20.
FDH coupled Demethylase qHTS protocol:

Three microliter enzyme mix (buffer + 200nM KDM5BDeltaAP final concentration) is dispensed into the assay plate using the BioRAPTR Flying Reagent Dispenser (FRD; Beckton-Dickenson). Compound (at various final concentration) and control solution is pin transferred to the assay plate using the Kalypsys 1536-pin tool apparatus. The assay plate is incubated for 10 min at room temperature followed by addition of 1uL substrate mix (buffer + 100uM ascorbic acid, 50uM ferrous ammonium sulfate, 12.5uM H3K4Me3, 25uM a-ketoglutarate, 0.25 mM NAD+, 0.25 U/mL formaldehyde dehydrogenase using the FRD yielding a total reaction volume of 4 uL. Initial fluorescence (Read1) is detected using the PerkinElmer ViewLux plate reader equipped with 340 nm excitation and 450 nm emission filters. The final fluorescence (Read2) signal is obtained after 30 min of room temperature incubation. Delta RFU is calculated (Read2 - Read1) and is used to generated dose response curves.

descr.name: Cell-based high-throughput assay to identify small molecules that inhibit phospholipid biosynthesis in animal cells 3: screen of the Enamine library.
description: This is a cell-based high-throughput to screen for antiviral compounds. A number of pathogenic viruses require host phospholipid biosynthesis for successful replication. The availability of small molecules which inhibit viral host phospholipid biosynthesis is an attractive approach as an antiviral treatment.

The screen supposes that inhibition of phospholipid biosynthesis in animal cells would result in reduced uptake and accumulation of exogenous fatty acids (used in phospholipid biosynthesis). Cells are treated with a test compound along with the fluorescent fatty acid. After 3 hours, unincorporated fluorescent fatty acid is removed and cells exposed to long-wavelength (>300 nm) UV light. The UV light excites the fluorescent moiety associated with the fatty acid within the cells, generating cytotoxic reactive oxygen species. Inhibition of phospholipid biosynthesis by any candidate compound should reduce uptake and accumulation of the fluorescent fatty acid, thus making the cells less sensitive to UV exposure, resulting in survival. Survival can be measured 24 hours later using standard protocols.
protocol: ZR-82 cells, a peroxisome-deficient variant of the wild-type CHO-K1 cell line, were plated into 384-well, clear bottom, black plates (Corning #3712 or #3764) at 1.25 x 103 cells/well in 20 ul Ham's F12 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum, penicillin G (100 U/ml) and streptomycin (75 U/ml). Plates were incubated overnight at 37 degrees C in 5% CO2. The next day, compounds dissolved in DMSO were diluted into medium and 2.8 ul of each diluted compound was added to the wells followed by 7ul of a cocktail containing A922500, a diacylglycerol acyltransferase 1 (DGAT-1) inhibitor, H2-003 a diacylglycerol acyltransferase 2 (DGAT-2) inhibitor, Sandoz 58-035, an acyl coenzyme A:cholesterol acyltransferase (ACAT) inhibitor, and the fluorescent fatty acid, 1-Pyrenedodecanoic acid (P12), resulting in a final concentration of 10 uM compound, 0.01% DMSO, 1 uM A922500, 5 uM Sandoz 58-035, 10 uM H2-003, and 20 uM P12 [1-O-[12-(1'-pyrene)]dodecanoic acid] in medium in each well. The compound tyrphostin AG-879, which this lab previously identified as an inhibitor of phospholipid and fatty acid biosynthesis (1), was used as a positive control and DMSO was the negative control. After a 3 hour incubation at 37 degrees C, the medium containing treatment was removed and replaced with 25 ul fresh medium to sequester any remaining P12 that was not incorporated into complex lipids in the cells. Plates were incubated for an additional 30 minutes at 37 degrees C, then cells were exposed to long-wavelength ultra-violet light through the bottom of the plate for 2-3 minutes by placing the clear bottom plates on borosilicate glass panes that were mounted 9 inches above a bank of four long-wavelength (>295nm) UV bulbs (Q lab, #UVA-340, 40 watts). The next day, cell viability was assessed by adding 5 ul of CellTiter Blue(R) (Promega) for 2 hours prior to reading the fluorescence intensity at 560 nm Ex/590 nm Em, on a Tecan plate reader.

1. Zoeller RA, Geoghegan-Barek K. 2019. A cell-based high-throughput screen identifies tyrphostin AG 879 as an inhibitor of animal cell phospholipid and fatty acid biosynthesis. Biochem Biophys Rep. 18: 100621. PMID: 30899803
comment: Candidate compounds were identified as "active" after displaying a difference of 2 standard deviations from negative control (DMSO) and similar results upon one or two repeated tests. All compounds were tested at 10 microM in tissue culture medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum.

descr.name: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) small molecule antagonists: colormetric cell-based qHTS assay
description: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences [NCATS]
National Institutes of Environmental Health Sciences [NIEHS]

Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the primary cholinesterase in the body that hydrolyzes a key neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. Inhibition of AChE activity can lead to neurotoxicity. The known inhibitors include organophosphorous pesticides (OP), chemical warfare agents, drugs, and various phytochemicals.

A homogenous cell-based assay using the Amplite Colormetric acetylcholinesterase assay kit (AAT Bioquest, Sunnyvale, CA) was used to evaluate the chemicals in the Tox21 10K library that inhibit AChE activity. The assay uses 5, 5-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB) to quantify the thiocholine produced from the hydrolysis of acetylthiocholine by AChE from the SH-SY5Y cells. AChE hydrolyses the acetylthiocholine to produce thiocholine that in turn reduces the DTNB, producing 5-thio-2-nitrobenzoic acid (TNB) which absorbs at 405 nm.
protocol: Tox21 Assay Protocol Summary:

For the cell-based AChE assay, 2,000 SH-SY5Y cells in 4 uL/well were dispensed into black, clear-bottom 1536-well plates using a Multidrop Combi dispenser (Thermo Scientific, MA). The assay plates were incubated overnight at 37 C to allow cells to attach to the wells, followed by the transfer of 23 nL of compound or DMSO (vehicle control) by a Pintool Station (Wako Automation, CA). The plates were incubated for 30 min at 37 C and 5% CO2, followed by the addition of 4 uL of detection cocktail solution (DTNB, acetylthiocholine) into each well using a Flying Reagent Dispenser (Beckman Coulter, CA) and then 90 min incubation at 37 C. Absorbance intensity (405 nm) was measured using an Envision plate reader (PerkinElmer, MA).

descr.name: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) small molecule antagonists: enzyme-based qHTS assay
description: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences [NCATS]
National Institutes of Environmental Health Sciences [NIEHS]

Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the primary cholinesterase in the body that hydrolyzes a key neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. Inhibition of AChE activity can lead to neurotoxicity. The known inhibitors include organophosphorous pesticides (OP), chemical warfare agents, drugs, and various phytochemicals.

An enzyme-based assay with the recombinant human AChE and Amplite Colormetric acetylcholinesterase assay kit (AAT Bioquest, Sunnyvale, CA) was used to evaluate the chemicals in the Tox21 10K library that inhibit AChE activity. The assay uses 5, 5-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB) to quantify the thiocholine produced from the hydrolysis of acetylthiocholine by AChE. AChE hydrolyses the acetylthiocholine to produce thiocholine that in turn reduces the DTNB, producing 5-thio-2-nitrobenzoic acid (TNB) which absorbs at 405 nm.
protocol: Tox21 Assay Protocol Summary:

For the enzyme-based AChE assay, recombinant human AChE (50 mU/mL) in 4 uL/well was dispensed into black, clear-bottom 1536-well plates using a Multidrop Combi dispenser (Thermo Scientific, MA). Then, 23 nL of compound or DMSO (vehicle control) was transferred into the assay plates by a Pintool Station (Wako Automation, CA). The plates were incubated for 30 min at room temperature, followed by the addition of 4 uL of colorimetric detection cocktail solution (DTNB, acetylthiocholine) into each well using a Flying Reagent Dispenser (Beckman Coulter, CA) and then 10 min incubation at room temperature. Absorbance intensity (405 nm) was measured using an Envision plate reader (PerkinElmer, MA).
comment: Disclaimer:

Although all reasonable efforts have been made to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data, caution should be exercised when interpreting the results as artifacts are possible from nonspecific effects such as assay signal interference. The curve fitting and activity calls presented here are based on the NCATS analysis methods. Alternative analysis methods and interpretations of the data are available at EPA (http://actor.epa.gov) and NTP (http://tools.niehs.nih.gov/cebs3/ui/).
Compound Ranking:

1. Compounds are first classified as having full titration curves, partial modulation, partial curve (weaker actives), single point activity (at highest concentration only), or inactive. See data field "Curve Description". For this assay, apparent inhibitors are ranked higher than compounds that showed apparent activation.

2. For all inactive compounds, PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE is 0. For all active compounds, a score range was given for each curve class type given above.  Active compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 40 and 100.  Inconclusive compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 1 and 39.  Fit_LogAC50 was used for determining relative score and was scaled to each curve class' score range.

descr.name: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) small molecule antagonists: fluorescence cell-based qHTS assay
description: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences [NCATS]
National Institutes of Environmental Health Sciences [NIEHS]

Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the primary cholinesterase in the body that hydrolyzes a key neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. Inhibition of AChE activity can lead to neurotoxicity. Known inhibitors of AChE include organophosphorous pesticides (OP), chemical warfare agents, drugs, and various phytochemicals.

A homogenous cell-based assay using Amplitetrade mark Fluorimetric Acetylcholinesterase Assay Kit *Green Fluorescence* (AAT Bioquest, Sunnyvale, CA) was used to evaluate the chemicals in the Tox21 10K library that inhibit AChE activity. The assay uses Thiolite Green to quantify the thiocholine produced from the hydrolysis of acetylthiocholine by AChE from the SH-SY5Y cells. AChE can hydrolyze acetylthiocholine to create thiocholine. Thiolite Green is fluorescent when reacting with thiocholine. It has spectral properties similar to those of fluorescein. The fluorescence intensity of Thiolite Green is used to measure AChE activity. Its signal can be easily read by a fluorescence microplate reader at Ex/Em = 490/520 nm.
protocol: Tox21 Assay Protocol Summary:

For cell-based AChE assay, 2,000 SH-SY5Y cells in 4 uL/well were dispensed into black, clear-bottom 1536-well plates using a Multidrop Combi (Thermo Scientific) dispenser. The assay plates were incubated overnight at 37 C to allow cells to attach to the wells, followed by the transfer of 23 nL compound or DMSO (vehicle control) by a Pintool station (Wako Automation, CA). The plates were incubated for 30 min at 37 C and 5% CO2, followed by the addition of 4 uL of detection cocktail solution (ThioliteGreen, acetylthiocholine) into each well using Flying Reagent Dispenser (Beckman Coulter, CA) and then following 40 min incubation at room temperature. Fluorescent intensity (Ex/Em = 490/520 nm) was measured using an Envision plate reader (PerkinElmer, MA).
comment: Disclaimer:

Although all reasonable efforts have been made to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data, caution should be exercised when interpreting the results as artifacts are possible from nonspecific effects such as assay signal interference. The curve fitting and activity calls presented here are based on the NCATS analysis methods. Alternative analysis methods and interpretations of the data are available at EPA (http://actor.epa.gov) and NTP (http://tools.niehs.nih.gov/cebs3/ui/).
Compound Ranking:

1. Compounds are first classified as having full titration curves, partial modulation, partial curve (weaker actives), single point activity (at highest concentration only), or inactive. See data field "Curve Description". For this assay, apparent inhibitors are ranked higher than compounds that showed apparent activation.

2. For all inactive compounds, PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE is 0. For all active compounds, a score range was given for each curve class type given above.  Active compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 40 and 100.  Inconclusive compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 1 and 39.  Fit_LogAC50 was used for determining relative score and was scaled to each curve class' score range.

descr.name: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) small molecule antagonists: enzyme-based qHTS assay with human liver microsomes
description: National Center for Advancing Translational Sciences [NCATS]
National Institutes of Environmental Health Sciences [NIEHS]

Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the primary cholinesterase in the body that hydrolyzes a key neurotransmitter, acetylcholine. Inhibition of AChE activity can lead to neurotoxicity. The known inhibitors include organophosphorous pesticides (OP), chemical warfare agents, drugs, and various phytochemicals. Some compounds like OP compounds may need metabolic activation to be active AChE inhibitors. The cytochrome P450 (CYP) superfamily in the human microsomes is responsible for the metabolism of various endogenous and exogenous compounds.

An enzyme-based assay with the recombinant human AChE, human liver microsomes and Amplite Colormetric acetylcholinesterase assay kit (AAT Bioquest, Sunnyvale, CA) was used to evaluate compounds in the Tox21 10K library that need metabolic activation for AChE inhibition. The assay uses 5, 5-dithiobis-(2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB) to quantify the thiocholine produced from the hydrolysis of acetylthiocholine by AChE. AChE hydrolyses the acetylthiocholine to produce thiocholine that in turn reduces the DTNB, producing 5-thio-2-nitrobenzoic acid (TNB) which absorbs at 405 nm.
protocol: Tox21 Assay Protocol Summary:

For the enzyme-based AChE assay with microsomes addition, a mixture of human AChE (50 mU/mL) and human liver microsomes (0.25 mg/mL, final concentration) in 3 uL/well was dispensed into black, clear-bottom 1536-well plates using a Multidrop Combi dispenser (Thermo Scientific, MA). Then, 23 nL of compound or DMSO (vehicle control) was transferred into the assay plates by a Pintool Station (Wako Automation, CA). Following compound addition, 1 uL of NADPH (0.25 mg/mL, final concentration) was transferred to the assay plate by a Flying Reagent Dispenser (Beckman Coulter, CA). The plates were incubated for 30 min at 37 C and 5% CO2, followed by the addition of 4 uL of colorimetric detection cocktail solution (DTNB, acetylthiocholine) into each well using a Flying Reagent Dispenser (Beckman Coulter, CA) and then 10 min incubation at room temperature. Absorbance intensity (405 nm) was measured using an Envision plate reader (PerkinElmer, MA).

1. Compounds are first classified as having full titration curves, partial modulation, partial curve (weaker actives), single point activity (at highest concentration only), or inactive. See data field "Curve Description". For this assay, apparent inhibitors are ranked higher than compounds that showed apparent activation.

2. For all inactive compounds, PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE is 0. For all active compounds, a score range was given for each curve class type given above.  Active compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 40 and 100.  Inconclusive compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 1 and 39.  Fit_LogAC50 was used for determining relative score and was scaled to each curve class' score range.

descr.name: ROC1-CUL1 CTD Inhibitor di-Ub FRET Primary HTS Screen
description: FRET based screen for finding small molecule inhibitors of ROC1-CUL1 CTD (C-terminal Domain) catalyzed Ubiquitination activiy. The production of Ub dimers formed between 2 Ub labelled with a fluorophore FRET pair is monitored by fluorescent plate reader.  Detected inhibitory effect may potentially be on any one of the Ubiquitin transfer steps between E1, E2 (Cdc34), and E3 (ROC1-CUL1 CTD).
protocol: The FRET K48 di-Ub assay described in Materials and Methods was optimized for an HTS in a 384-well assay format, using three reagent addition steps. Library compounds, stored in 10mM stock plates (DMSO), were transferred into assay plates and each well contains a single compound at 100muM in 1mul 10% DMSO. The complete complement of proteins/enzymes (6.5mul), containing Ub E1 (14nM), E2 Cdc34 (124nM), E3 ROC1-CUL1 CTD (0.2muM), Ub C31-I555 (donor, 0.93muM), and Ub C64-I647 (receptor, 1.62muM), in the presence of 33mM Tris-HCl (pH7.4), 1.7mM MgCl2, 0.33mM DTT, and BSA (0.07mg/ml), was added to each plate. To initiate ubiquitination, ATP (2.5mul in 2.64mM) was added and its final concentration was 0.66mM. The concentration of ATP was set high to minimize identification of nucleotide analogues because the priority of the HTS is to find small molecule modulators specific for E3 ROC1-CUL1 CTD. In this setting, the concentration of compound and DMSO in a given well were 10muM and 1%, respectively. After incubation at room temperature for 45min, EDTA (30mM) was added to terminate the reaction. The reaction was quantified based on the ratio of acceptor:donor fluorescence (excitation 515nm; donor emission 570nm; acceptor emission 670nm) using an EnSpire plate reader (Perkin Elmer).
comment: A cutoff of NPI (Normalized percentage of Inhibition) >/= 25 was used to score the "hits".  All compounds scoring >/= 25 was marked "active" and all below 25 was marked "inactive"

descr.name: qHTS Primary assay for Inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum Dd2 growth in vitro
description: Malaria, a parasitic disease spread to humans through the bite of a Plasmodium infected Anopheles mosquito, continues to be a global health burden affecting millions of people, with an estimated 228 million cases and 405,000 deaths in 2018. Concerns about safety and limitations of current antimalarial treatments strongly emphasize the need to develop new therapeutic options. The scarce number of chemotypes and validated drug targets with efficacy against the liver stage, have hindered development of new antimalarials. To address this, a chemoprophylactic drug discovery effort was conducted through a combined phenotypic high-throughput asexual blood stage and liver stage screen, providing a robust foundation to identify liver-stage active lead chemotypes. Compounds were initially screened against Plasmodium falciparum Dd2 strain parasites using a in vitro SYBRGreen-1 based 72 hr proliferation assay to identify novel chemotypes to advance to liver stage assays.

descr.name: Antagonist identification of Pyk2 oligomerization: high-throughput screening cellular assay
description: Data Source: Conrad Prebys Center for Chemical Genomics (CPCCG)
Source Affiliation: Sanford-Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (SBP, San Diego, CA)
Network: NCI funded grants for translational research
Assay Provider: Joseph Loftus, PhD, Mayo Clinic, Scottsdale, AZ; Eduard Sergienko, PhD, SBP, La Jolla, CA.

Pyk2 is non-receptor protein-tyrosine kinase from the focal adhesion kinase (FAK) family involved in control of reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, cell adhesion, polarization and migration. Pyk2 is upregulated in glioblastoma (GB) cells and high levels are associated with more invasive phenotype and metastasis. The aggressive invasion of GB in the brain makes complete surgical resection impossible, increases the resistance to radiation and chemotherapy, and virtually assures tumor recurrence.  Conversely, inhibition or knockdown of Pyk2 reduces invasiveness and increases survival in GB xenograft animals.  Small molecules targeting the Pyk2 kinase domain has proven difficult due to off target kinase activity.  As an alternative to Pyk2 kinase domain inhibition, we have targeted the oligomerization of Pyk2 that occurs through N-terminal FERM domain interactions and is required for the kinase activity. We have developed a live cell luminescent assay monitoring oligomerization of Pyk2-FERM domains using NanoBiT complementation approach and screened 100K compounds to identify inhibitors of Pyk2 activation.
protocol: A. Brief Description of the Assay

This Pyk2 FERM oligomerization assay we developed utilizes the NanoLuc(R) Binary Technology (NanoBiT(R)) reporter system based on structural complementation between a Large BiT (LgBiT; 18kDa) subunit and a small complimentary peptide, Small BiT (SmBiT; 11 amino acid peptide). We have generated a Q293 clonal cell line which expresses SmBiT-Pyk2FERM-GFP domain and LgBiT-Pyk2FERM-RFP.  This assay was performed on live Q293 cells in 1536-well format using Corning white 1536-well plates (cat #3727) on a Viewluxtrade mark plate reader (Perkin Elmer).
B. Assay reagent components:
1.#Cell growth media consisting of DMEM (Corning 15-017), 10% FBS, 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin, 1% L-Glutamine
2.#TrypLE Express cell detachment reagent (ThermoFisher 12605036)
3.#Assay media consisting of Opti-MEM (Gibco) 11058-021, 4% FBS, 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin, 1% L-Glutamine
4.#Promega Nano-Glo(R) Live Cell Assay System which has a cell permeant NanoLuc(R) substrate, furimazine, and live cell dilution buffer (Promega N2012)
5.#5 mM small molecule compound stock solutions dissolved in 100% DMSO and dispensed using Echo(R) Labcyte acoustic dispenser
C. Step-by-step protocol:
1.#Dispense 5 uL of Q293 SmBiT-FERM/LgBiT-FERM cells into columns 1-48
2.#Incubate lidded plates at 37 degrees C 5% CO2 SteriStoretrade mark (HighRes Biosolutions) for 16h
3.#Reagent dispenses
a.#Dispense 25 nL compound aliquots to the wells in columns 5-48
b.#Dispense 25 nL DMSO aliquots to the wells in columns 2-4
c.#Dispense 25nL positive control to the wells in column 1
4.#Incubate lidded plates between 2 x 384 plates filled with water, covered in plastic wrap for 2 hours at 37 degrees C and 5% CO2.
5.#Dispense 1 uL of NanoGlo(R) detection reagent diluted 1:25 in LCS into columns 1-48
6.#Incubate for between 5-30 minutes at room temperature and proceed to measure luminescent signal using ViewLuxtrade mark plate reader
D. Final concentration of reagents in the assay wells
1.#1:125 dilution of NanoGlo(R) live cell substrate
2.#25 uM small molecule compounds (wells in columns 5-44)
3.#0.5% DMSO (all wells)

1. Negative control in columns 2-4
2. Positive control in columns 1
3. Test wells in columns 5-48

Due to the nature of the loss-of-signal assay, antagonist compounds demonstrate negative Z-score values. Compounds with Z-score  -3 are defined as actives in this assay.

b.#If Z-score is < -5, then Activity Score is assigned 40;

descr.name: Primary qHTS assay for inhibitors of Activation Induced Cytidine Deaminase (AID): AID signal
description: National Institute of Health (NIH), Bethesda, MD

Activation-Induced Deaminase (AID) is a cytosine deaminase which converts cytosine into uracil within stretches of ssDNA. The presence of uracil in DNA initiates a cascade of mutagenic DNA repair to introduce point mutations and DNA double strand breaks. Specific targeting of AID to the immunoglobulin heavy chain loci (Igh) promotes mutagenesis in the antibody variable region for somatic hypermutation (SHM) or switch regions leading to class switch recombination (CSR). However, AID also plays a role in accumulating unnecessary mutations across the genome. Mis-targeting of AID results in the initiation of tumor development and leads to greater drug resistance among cancer cells when continually expressed. To identify an AID inhibitor, a small molecule library will be screened in collaboration with NCATS core facility at NIH. To confirm biological function, inhibitors will be examined in an in vitro murine B-cell activation assay and subsequent secondary validation screens. Top molecules will be further screened to identify inhibitory efficacy against a wild type primary splenocytes assay. Using these approaches, we hope to identify a small molecule with great efficacy and low toxicity for use as a molecular probe to further characterize AID's intricacies, or even as a therapeutic.

A FRET based analysis of cytosine deamination, was developed to identify potential inhibitors of AID catalytic activity. This screen has two signal output, Read 1 evaluates the AID inhibition response. The second readout (Read 2) evaluates UDG response and is uses as a counterscreen to exclude false positive inhibitors. Inhibition in AID and inactivity in the UDG signal is the desired outcome for this assay.

description: National Institute of Health (NIH), Bethesda, MD

Activation-Induced Deaminase (AID) is a cytosine deaminase which converts cytosine into uracil within stretches of ssDNA. The presence of uracil in DNA initiates a cascade of mutagenic DNA repair to introduce point mutations and DNA double strand breaks. Specific targeting of AID to the immunoglobulin heavy chain loci (Igh) promotes mutagenesis in the antibody variable region for somatic hypermutation (SHM) or switch regions leading to class switch recombination (CSR). However, AID also plays a role in accumulating unnecessary mutations across the genome. Mis-targeting of AID results in the initiation of tumor development and leads to greater drug resistance among cancer cells when continually expressed. To identify an AID inhibitor, a small molecule library will be screened in collaboration with NCATS core facility at NIH. To confirm biological function, inhibitors will be examined in an in vitro murine B-cell activation assay and subsequent secondary validation screens. Top molecules will be further screened to identify inhibitory efficacy against a wild type primary splenocytes assay. Using these approaches, we hope to identify a small molecule with great efficacy and low toxicity for use as a molecular probe to further characterize AID's intricacies, or even as a therapeutic.

A FRET based analysis of cytosine deamination, was developed to identify potential inhibitors of AID catalytic activity. This screen has two signal output, Read 1 evaluates the AID inhibition response. The second readout (Read 2) evaluates UDG response and is uses as a counterscreen to exclude false positive inhibitors. Inhibition in AID and inactivity in the UDG signal is the desired outcome for this assay.

Disclaimer:

Although all reasonable efforts have been made to ensure the accuracy and reliability of the data, caution should be exercised when interpreting the results as artifacts are possible from nonspecific effects such as assay signal interference. The curve fitting and activity calls presented here are based on the NCATS analysis methods.
Compound Ranking:

1. Compounds are first classified as having full titration curves, partial modulation, partial curve (weaker actives), single point activity (at highest concentration only), or inactive. For this assay, apparent inhibitors are ranked higher than compounds that showed apparent activation.

2. For all inactive compounds, with a ratio activity curve class of 4, PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE is 0. For all active compounds, a score range was given for each curve class type given above. Active compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 40 and 100. For a ratio activity curve class = -1.1, score = 80+abs((log_ac50+4.5)*inf_activity/20). For ratio.curve_class == -1.2 && abs(ratio.max_response) > 6*10, score = 60+abs((log_ac50+4.5)*inf_activity/20). For ratio.curve_class == -2.1 || ( ratio.curve_class==-2.2 && abs(ratio.max_response) > 6*10), score = 40+abs((log_ac50+4.5)*inf_activity/20). For ratio.curve_class == -1.2 || ratio.curve_class == -2.2, score = 20+abs((log_ac50+4.5)*inf_activity/20). Inconclusive compounds, with a donor curve class other than 4, have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE of 10. Inconclusive compounds have PUBCHEM_ACTIVITY_SCORE between 1 and 39.

descr.name: Rucaparib conditional oncology-focused drug screen on ovarian cancer cells.
description: Background: Homologous recombination deficiencies (HRD) are present in
approximately half of epithelial ovarian cancers, for which PARP inhibitors (PARPi) are
becoming a preferred treatment option. However, a considerable proportion of these
carcinomas acquire resistance or harbour de novo resistance, posing a significant
Methods: To identify new combinatorial therapeutics to overcome resistance to PARPi,
we employed high-throughput conditional RNAi and drug screening of patient-derived
ovarian cancer cells. To prioritise clinically relevant drug combinations, we queried The
Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and Genomics of Drug Sensitivity in Cancer (GDSC)
project with the candidate targets and their respective drugs to reach three main
Findings: Firstly, we found that rucaparib enhanced the effect of BET inhibitors
(CPI-203 & CPI-0610) irrespective of clinical subtype or HRD status. Dasatinib, a non-
receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, augmented the synergy of rucaparib and BET
inhibitors, proposing a potential broadly applicable triple-drug combination for high-grade
serous and clear cell ovarian carcinomas. Secondly, rucaparib synergised with the BCL2
family inhibitor navitoclax, with preferential activity in ovarian carcinomas that harbour
alterations in BRCA1/2, BARD1, or MSH2/6. Thirdly, we identified potentially
antagonistic drug combinations between the PARPi rucaparib and vinca alkaloids,
anthracyclines, and antimetabolites, cautioning their use in the clinic.
Interpretation: These findings illuminate new insights into PARP inhibitor resistance
and propose novel therapeutic combinations that could benefit broader populations of
protocol: The 395-compound library was purchased from Selleck Chemicals and targets a broad
range of cancer-related pathways. Drugs were diluted to an 8-
point dose curve incorporating a 3-fold dilution step. The highest final drug concentrations
were 5 muM; DMSO or PBS remained consistent across the wells at 0.05%. Cells were
seeded at ~30% confluence in 384-well microtiter plates. The next day, drugs were added
using a CyBio FeliX liquid handler (Analytik Jena AG), and cells were further incubated for
an additional 144 h. Cell viability was determined using CellTiter-Glo(R) 2.0 and a BioTek
H4 Synergy plate reader. Single agent responses were normalized to the solvent
concentration (either 0.05% PBS or DMSO) while the combination drug responses were
normalized to the solvent concentration and 10 uM of rucaparib. Z factors were calculated
for each microtiter plate to ensure adequate screening quality.
comment: A tested drug concentration is considered active when it has a normalized percent viability less than 100%.

descr.name: Stabilization of p53 in human papillomavirus-positive cells
description: The p53 protein regulates cell cycle and functions as a tumor suppressor, playing a significant role in the majority of all human cancers. In human papillomavirus (HPV)-infected cells, p53 is targeted for degradation by a protein complex formed by the viral oncoprotein E6 and the cellular ubiquitin-ligase E6AP. This is necessary for HPV-infected cell survival, as p53 would accumulate in response to the replication stress signals provoked by the HPV E7 oncoprotein. For this screen, we engineered a high-risk HPV-18 positive human cervical cancer cell line (HeLa) to stably express a transcriptionally inactive mutant p53(R273C) fused to a monomeric variant of the red fluorescent protein eqFP61 (mRuby). The stability of this fusion protein is governed by p53(R273C), thus becoming a fluorescent reporter for p53 stability in vivo. In addition, p53(R273C) functions in a dominant negative manner, interfering with endogenous p53 activity. This enables us to perform screens for small molecules that stabilize p53 in HPV-positive cancer cells without inducing p53-dependent apoptosis.
This screen was conducted by the lab of Dr. Peter Howley (Harvard Medical School) at the ICCB-Longwood Screening Facility, Harvard Medical School.
protocol: Prior to screening, HeLa cells were transduced with a lentivirus carrying the vector PHAGE-N CMVt N-RIG3 p53(R273C) encoding constitutively expressed SGFP2 fused to histone 2B and mRuby-p53(R273C). Following transduction, the cells were selected using neomycin and fluorescent activated cell sorting. The day before the compound treatment, cells were plated (750 cells/well) in a final volume of 30 L/well of Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% (v/v) fetal bovine serum using a Thermo Combi. Plates were spun for 45 s at 500 rpm and incubated overnight (~24 h) at 37 degrees C, 5% CO2.

On the day of the screening, 33 nL of each compound was transferred to assay wells via a custom pin-transfer workstation. Additionally, 33 nL of positive (Velcade 300 M) and negative (DMSO 100%) controls were transferred to each plate into the corresponding columns that did not contain experimental compounds. For every compound library plate, there were two daughter plates (A and B). Plates were stacked 5 high, covered with lids, and incubated at 37 degrees C for 24h and 48h.

Assay plates were read using an Acumen Laser Scanning Cytometer 24h and 48h after compound treatment, using the following settings: For SGFP2 (channel 2), the 488 nm laser was used, with 6 mW output, 600 voltage gain and sensitivity threshold at 1; and for mRuby (channel 3), the 561 nm laser was used, with 8 mW output, 600 voltage gain and sensitivity threshold at 1.
comment: Total nuclei and %p53 positive was calculated for all wells at 24 and 48h using the Cellista software. Percentage of p53 positive cells values were normalized to the positive and negative controls to determine a normalized percent of p53 activation. This was done on a per plate basis. The proteasome inhibitor Velcade (Adipogen, AG-CR1-3602-M005) at 330 nM was used as positive control while only the vehicle (DMSO, Sigma, D8418, 0.1% final concentration) was used as negative control. From these values the following normalized values were calculated (for both 24h and 48h): Normalized total nuclei = (total nuclei in experimental well / plate average negative control total nuclei) * 100. Normalized %p53 positive = (%p53 positive in experimental well - plate average negative control %p53 positive cells) / (plate average positive control %p53 positive cells - plate average negative control %p53 positive cells) * 100.

Based on the normalized percent p53 positive values, a compound was considered active when replicate average normalized % p53 positive cells > 50% for either or both time points. Activity scores were based on the replicate average normalized %p53 positive cells at 24hr. Values less than 0 were set to 0, and values > 100 were set to 100 (100% activity). Compounds with an activity score > 50 were considered active; some compounds were scored active despite having an activity score < 50 since % p53 positive cells was > 50% only at 48hr.
The average normalized total nuclei values were categorized as:
Very Low: x < 25%
Medium: 50% < X > 75%
High: x < 75%
The average normalized % of p53 positive cells values were categorized as:
Low: x < 25%
Medium: 25% < X > 50%
Strong: 50% < X > 75%
Very Strong: x < 75%
Compounds that scored as strong or very strong in this classification (at either time point) were selected for follow up.

descr.name: Cell-based high throughput primary assay to identify activators of GPR151
description: Source: The Scripps Research Institute Molecular Screening Center (SRIMSC)
Center Affiliation: The Scripps Research Institute
Assay Provider: The Scripps Research Institute
Grant Proposal PI: Patricia McDonald, The Scripps Research Institute
Name: Cell-based high throughput primary assay to identify activators of GPR151

The orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR151 has a distinctive distribution pattern in mammalian brains, with highly specific enrichment in a small bilateral brain structure known as the habenula complex. This structure sends projections to the dopaminergic striatum and receives inputs from the limbic forebrain, modulating cross-talk between these brain regions. It is therefore ideally located, both anatomically and functionally, to regulate emotional, motivational and cognitive behaviors. Consequently, it is believed that the habenula plays a critically important role in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia, depression and drug dependence. The restricted and unique brain expression pattern of GPR151 suggests a role for this receptor in regulating the habenula complex and thus affecting such disorders. In this proposal we will implement and miniaturize a HTS-compatible cell-based functional assay to facilitate the identification of potent GPR151-selective small molecule molecular probes. These molecules will then be optimized and used to interrogate GPR151's role in regulating the habenula complex and the impact of GPR151 modulation upon both normal physiological processes and disease states.

TThe goal of this NIH sponsored research project was to identify GPR151 agonists via high-throughput screening (HTS) efforts. In brief, the McDonald Lab transferred the GPR151 AG 384wpf assay to Scripps for implementation and miniaturization to 1,536-well format followed by screening against the Scripps Drug Discovery Library (SDDL). This project was aided by cheminformatic efforts to help identify compounds that demonstrated authentic agonist pharmacology and non-promiscuous activity profiles across other primary screens run against the SDDL. Name: Cell-based high throughput counterscreen assay to identify off target activators of GPR151

The orphan G protein-coupled receptor GPR151 has a distinctive distribution pattern in mammalian brains, with highly specific enrichment in a small bilateral brain structure known as the habenula complex. This structure sends projections to the dopaminergic striatum and receives inputs from the limbic forebrain, modulating cross-talk between these brain regions. It is therefore ideally located, both anatomically and functionally, to regulate emotional, motivational and cognitive behaviors. Consequently, it is believed that the habenula plays a critically important role in the pathophysiology of neuropsychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia, depression and drug dependence. The restricted and unique brain expression pattern of GPR151 suggests a role for this receptor in regulating the habenula complex and thus affecting such disorders. In this proposal we will implement and miniaturize a HTS-compatible cell-based functional assay to facilitate the identification of potent GPR151-selective small molecule molecular probes. These molecules will then be optimized and used to interrogate GPR151's role in regulating the habenula complex and the impact of GPR151 modulation upon both normal physiological processes and disease states.

protocol: Assay Overview:

A counterscreen assay, employing GPR119 cells, was also implemented by Scripps to identify compounds that non-specifically affect the PathHunter detection method. The purpose of this assay is to counterscreen and determine the selective activity of compounds identified as active in a set of previous experiments entitled, "Cell-based high throughput primary assay to identify activators of GPR151". In this assay, stably transfected cells expressing GPR119 and the B-arrestin pathhunter reporter are incubated with test compounds. As designed, test compounds that act as activators of GPR119 activity will increase luminescence signal. Compounds are tested in triplicate at a nominal test concentration of 11.2 micromolar.

At this stage 3uL of Promega Beta-Glo detection Buffer was added to all wells followed by a 1 hour incubation at room temperature. descr.name: Primary qHTS for Identification of Small Molecule Inhibitors of Huntingtin Promoter Activity
description: Assay Provider: Russell L. Margolis M.D.
Department Neurology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD

Huntington's Disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in exon 1 of huntingtin (HTT). While there are currently no disease-modifying treatments for HD, recent efforts have focused on development of nucleotide-based therapeutics to lower HTT expression. As an alternative to siRNA or oligonucleotide methods, we hypothesized that suppression of HTT expression might be accomplished by small molecules that either (1) directly decrease HTT expression by suppressing HTT promoter activity or (2) indirectly decrease HTT expression by increasing the promoter activity of HTT-AS, the gene antisense to HTT that appears to inhibit expression of HTT.

We developed and employed a high throughput screen for modifiers of HTT and HTT-AS promoter activity using luminescent reporter HEK293 cells; of the 52,041 compounds tested, we identified 898 replicable hits. We used a rigorous stepwise approach to assess compound toxicity and the capacity of the compounds to specifically lower huntingtin protein in 5 different cell lines, including HEK293 cells, HD lymphoblastoid cells, mouse primary neurons, HD iPSCs differentiated into cortical-like neurons, and HD hESCs. We found no compounds which were able to lower huntingtin without lowering cell viability in all assays, though the potential efficacy of a few compounds at non-toxic doses could not be excluded. Our results suggest that more specific targets may facilitate a small molecule approach to HTT suppression.

descr.name: Primary qHTS for Identification of Small Molecule Activators of Huntingtin-Antisense Promoter Activity
description: Assay Provider: Russell L. Margolis M.D.
Department Neurology, Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine, Baltimore, MD

Huntington's Disease (HD) is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by a CAG repeat expansion in exon 1 of huntingtin (HTT). While there are currently no disease-modifying treatments for HD, recent efforts have focused on development of nucleotide-based therapeutics to lower HTT expression. As an alternative to siRNA or oligonucleotide methods, we hypothesized that suppression of HTT expression might be accomplished by small molecules that either (1) directly decrease HTT expression by suppressing HTT promoter activity or (2) indirectly decrease HTT expression by increasing the promoter activity of HTT-AS, the gene antisense to HTT that appears to inhibit expression of HTT.

We developed and employed a high throughput screen for modifiers of HTT and HTT-AS promoter activity using luminescent reporter HEK293 cells; of the 52,041 compounds tested, we identified 898 replicable hits. We used a rigorous stepwise approach to assess compound toxicity and the capacity of the compounds to specifically lower huntingtin protein in 5 different cell lines, including HEK293 cells, HD lymphoblastoid cells, mouse primary neurons, HD iPSCs differentiated into cortical-like neurons, and HD hESCs. We found no compounds which were able to lower huntingtin without lowering cell viability in all assays, though the potential efficacy of a few compounds at non-toxic doses could not be excluded. Our results suggest that more specific targets may facilitate a small molecule approach to HTT suppression.
